summary: Neo is an agentic program-analysis framework that finds privilege-escalation bugs across polyglot microservices: an LLM agent plans analyses and judges semantics (which operations are privileged, whether authN/authZ checks are adequate) while CodeQL-backed, language-agnostic 'code search primitives' (AST, flow, call-graph, inter-service channel queries over REST/gRPC/Kafka/etc.) retrieve precise context. Evaluated on 25 open-source microservice apps (7 languages, Java-heavy), it reports 24 zero-day privilege escalations plus 18 other zero-days and beats CodeQL, MScan and the EnIGMA bash-based agent.

claims.claim: 81.0% precision and 85.0% recall on a ground-truth dataset.
claims.evidence: §VI-B and Table VI: 17 TP / 4 FP over 20 verified vulns in 4 apps. Caveat: 2 of the 20 ground-truth vulns were found by Neo itself (Table III), which mildly inflates recall; 18 are prior CVEs. Single default config (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, T=0.2).

claims.claim: Neo found 24 zero-day privilege escalation vulnerabilities (42 total incl. extensibility study), responsibly disclosed.
claims.evidence: §VI-B: 39 TP of 51 reports, 24 new; manual verification with PoC exploits; §VI-H: 18 of 42 acknowledged, 8 patched at submission. Externally checkable via disclosure.

§VI-D: on a 44-vuln union set, Neo 39, EnIGMA 15 (14 FP), CodeQL* 7 (53.8% prec.), MScan*+Sinks 16 vs Neo 19 on Java subset. Baselines are augmented with Neo's validator (fairer), EnIGMA given same prompt/docs/10h budget. Union-of-detections ground truth is standard but biased toward the tool that contributes most findings; EnIGMA still found 2 Neo missed.

claims.claim: Structured code-search primitives (vs raw bash/file reading) are essential; without them most vulns are missed.
claims.evidence: §VI-C ablations: application-specific privileged ops raise recall 33.3%→92.9%; validation removes 62.2% of FPs (135→51 flows); EnIGMA failures attributed to context exhaustion (DeathStarBench flows spanning >35 functions).

claims.claim: Practical cost: ~1.6 h and ~18 USD per application.
claims.evidence: §VI-E: 38.9 h total for 25 apps; EnIGMA ~3.4 h, ~25 USD.

patterns.note: Deterministic static-analysis (CodeQL) retrieval primitives beat bash/grep file-reading agent (EnIGMA) on large polyglot codebases; ablation shows primitives essential.
Call graphs, data-flow graphs and inter-service channel graphs are the context substrate; evidence from ablation and baseline comparison.
Cross-service (cross-repo-like) flow tracing via channel identifiers (URLs, topics) across REST/gRPC/Kafka/RabbitMQ/Dubbo; 25 apps.
Static-analysis output drives the agent loop; LLM handles semantics, analysis handles structure.
LLM-generated SMT-LIB path constraints pruned 15 of 135 flows (all true negatives on manual check); constraints generated for only 28 flows.
LLM authZ validation removed 69 flows; only 10 sampled for manual audit (all correct) — small validation sample.
Real open-source applications with responsibly disclosed, partially patched findings.

methodology.sample: 25 open-source microservice apps (21 evaluation corpus with ≥500 stars, 4 ground-truth apps with 20 vulns), 6.2M LoC, 7 languages.
methodology.baselines: CodeQL default critical suite, MScan (Java only), EnIGMA (SWE-agent-based security agent); baselines augmented with Neo's validation for fairness.
methodology.models: Claude 3.7 Sonnet default (T=0.2); sensitivity on ground-truth set with Gemini 2.5 Flash and GPT-5 mini across T∈{0..1}.
methodology.variance: No repeated runs/seeds on the main evaluation; temperature sweep shows high sensitivity (Fig. 5) but single run per point.
methodology.ablations: Privileged-op identification, search primitives vs direct CodeQL, validation strategies, prompting (few-shot/CoT) — Tables V–VI, Fig. 6.
methodology.contamination_controls: In-context examples drawn from apps outside the dataset; no control for prior CVEs being in model training data (ground-truth CVEs are public).
methodology.languages: Go, Java, JS, Python, C#, C, C++; Java dominant in corpus and ground truth.

standards.peer_review: Accepted at IEEE S&P 2026 (meta-review included in appendix).
standards.artifacts: Code and prompts at github.com/columbia/neo (stated in §V).

biases.detail: Authors manually verify their own tool's reports and construct the union comparison set; 2 of 20 ground-truth vulns are Neo's own finds.
Main results are single runs at T=0.2 despite Fig. 5 showing strong temperature/model sensitivity.
Ground-truth vulns are public CVEs that may be in model pretraining data; recall on them may overstate zero-day capability.
LLM authN/authZ validator that discards 69 flows validated on only 10 sampled cases.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Claude 3.7 Sonnet (default), Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5 mini as backbones; CodeQL as substrate. No author vendor affiliation.
coi.funding: NSF grants CNS-21-54404 and CNS-20-46361, gifts from Google, Columbia funds.
coi.detail: Google gift funding while Gemini is one of three models in a sensitivity study (not favored; default is Claude). Academic authors evaluating their own tool, as is standard.

verdict_reason: Peer-reviewed at a top venue, real polyglot (Java-heavy) codebases, externally verifiable disclosed zero-days, reasonable baselines including a bash-based agent, ablations, and released code/prompts. Weaknesses (single runs, union ground truth, small LLM-validator audit) are typical and disclosed, not fatal.
applicability: Strongly relevant as architecture evidence even though the task is security: a Java backend team whose ingestion spans ≥4 services/repos benefits from the same split — deterministic, compiler-grade code queries (CodeQL/LSP/static analysis) exposed as a few typed tools to the agent, with cross-service links resolved from channel identifiers (REST paths, Kafka topics). It argues against relying on grep/file-reading alone in a multi-repo Java estate. Directly reusable as a security gate for domain content services (authZ on content-publishing endpoints). Caveats: needs per-repo CodeQL databases (build step per Java repo), 10-hour budgets, and ~18 USD/app; host-agnostic Python orchestration so it fits mixed agent hosts as an offline job rather than an in-editor tool. Says nothing about spec-driven development.
